paras: The attempted lynching of Charles Gant took place at the Grand Army of the Republic state reunion grounds in Lincoln, Nebraska, on the evening of Friday, August 17, 1900, when a white mob of several hundred tried to seize Gant, a Black man, from police. Gant was accused of striking a special officer, Mart Howe, over the head with a billiard cue. Police beat back the mob with clubs and took Gant to jail, and he was later bound over to the district court.
The reunion of Union veterans closed that Friday night; Howe, a special officer at the grounds, was described in an early dispatch as "a prominent politician and a Grand Army man."

According to the wire account, Gant created a disturbance on the grounds and Howe reprimanded him; an earlier dispatch said Howe put him out of the pavilion. Gant was said to have taken a billiard cue from a boy, come up behind Howe and knocked him down with a blow to the head that cut his scalp and left him unconscious. He ran, pursued by a squad of officers and "a hundred or more angry white men," and was caught after a chase of more than a mile, standing waist-deep in a swamp.

When the prisoner was brought back to the grounds, a mob of several hundred whites formed and charged the police to get hold of him. A rope was taken from a reunion tent, and the crowd shouted "Lynch him" and "Kill the nigger." The police surrounded Gant, beat back the mob with their clubs and hurried him off the grounds to jail. The Lincoln weekly Nebraska Independent wrote that he "only escaped lynching by the desperate efforts of the officers, assisted by several negroes who were there."

The wire reported that Gant was charged with assault with intent to kill, while the Independent said he would be charged with assault with intent to do great bodily injury once Howe was out of danger. Nearly two weeks later Howe was still in a "semi-dazed condition," and Gant's preliminary examination was set twice without result; the Independent reported that Gant meant to make "a vigorous defense." By early September the German-language Nebraska Staats-Anzeiger reported that he had been bound over to the district court.

Around September 12, Judge Frost heard an application to free Gant on bail, with police officer Tom Carnahan, described as Gant's uncle, and Belt Hawkins offered as sureties. The court found Hawkins's property barely equal to his exemptions and, since the law required two good sureties, kept Gant in jail. No report of arrests among the mob or of a trial verdict appears in the coverage.

The first wire stories, dated August 18 and 19, reported only the assault, under headlines such as "Tough Negro May Be a Murderer" in the Rock Island Argus and "Assaulted by a Negro" in a South Dakota weekly. The mob scene appeared in a Lincoln dispatch datelined August 20, which the Topeka State Journal printed that day as "Negro Mobbed in Lincoln. Knocked a Policeman Down and Was Almost Lynched." Lincoln's own Independent gave the episode a single paragraph that called Gant "a vicious colored man" and predicted he would "probably get a term in the pen."

In the Black press the story appeared only as the same wire, in two Kansas weeklies on August 24. The Topeka Colored Citizen ran it under the same headline as the Topeka State Journal, capitalizing "Negro," and kept the mob's cry of "Kill the Nigger." The Kansas City American Citizen ran it without a headline, directly after a New York report of Black residents seeking legal action against police after the riots there. Neither Black paper added comment, and the role of Black bystanders in protecting Gant appeared only in the Lincoln weekly.

The wire that reported the mob was datelined August 20 and tied the riot to "the closing of the state reunion," without giving a day. The August 18 dispatch dated the assault to "last evening," and the Independent placed it on Friday evening and said the reunion closed Friday night, which puts the events on August 17.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Gant
bases: A white mob of several hundred took a rope, cried 'Lynch him' and charged police to seize a Black prisoner accused of striking an officer; police held them off, so this was an attempted lynching (A2, A4, A5).

Gant was not killed: police beat back the mob and jailed him (A2, A6), and he was later bound over and held for trial (A9, A10). The mob of several hundred acted without authority on the accusation that he had struck an officer, which makes this an attempted, not a completed, lynching (A2, A4).
The Aug. 20 wire (A2, A5, A6) and the local Nebraska Independent (A4) independently report that Gant was chased, brought back and narrowly saved from lynching by officers.

accounts.label: Wire report (Lincoln, Aug. 20)
accounts.gist: A riot and attempted lynching marked the reunion's close: a chase of over a mile, a mob of several hundred whites charging police, a rope and cries of 'Lynch him'; police clubbed the mob back and jailed Gant, charged with assault with intent to kill.

accounts.label: Lincoln weekly (Nebraska Independent)
accounts.gist: Gant, 'a vicious colored man,' cut Howe's scalp with a billiard cue Friday evening; he escaped lynching only through the officers' efforts, aided by several Black men, and would be charged with assault with intent to do great bodily injury.

accounts.label: Earlier wires (Aug. 18-19)
accounts.gist: Reported only the assault on Howe in the reunion pavilion and Gant's arrest after a long chase, with Howe unconscious; no mob is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Topeka State Journal ran the wire the day it was datelined under 'Negro Mobbed in Lincoln. Knocked a Policeman Down and Was Almost Lynched.'
The Nebraska Independent called Gant 'a vicious colored man' and predicted 'a term in the pen,' while crediting the officers and 'several negroes' with preventing a lynching.
Earlier wires headed 'Tough Negro May Be a Murderer' and 'Assaulted by a Negro' framed the story as a Black man's attack on a prominent Grand Army man.

The Colored Citizen reprinted the wire with the same headline, capitalizing 'Negro'; the American Citizen ran it unheaded beneath a report of New York Black residents organizing against police after riots.
